decision.explanation: The solid cylinder has vertical bounds 0 ≤ z ≤ 3 and projects onto the disk x² + y² ≤ 9. Thus D is defined by x²/9 + y²/9 ≤ 1.

after.worked_solution:
A typical three-dimensional type I region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094056/assets/05f940e247c6cd5d862d81fc3a34658353bef5513dfe862bbc67a120c0345838.png)

First, we have that $z$ is bounded below by $0$ and above by $3.$ So, the type I representation of $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,0\le z\le 3\,}.
$$

Now, that base curve in the $xy$-plane of the cylinder's surface is the circle $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1$ centered at $(0,0).$ Therefore, the domain $D$ is given by the following disc:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}\,\,\le \,\,1}.
$$

decision.explanation: Since x²+y²=r²=9 and r≥0, the surface has r=3. A full revolution uses 0≤θ<2π, and the height satisfies 0≤z≤3. Thus C=[0,2π)×[0,3].

after.worked_solution:
The position of a point in cylindrical polar coordinates is written as $(r,\theta ,z),$ where

* $r\ge 0$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

* $z\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

The heater is a circular cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis of symmetry is the $z$-axis.

We note the following:

* Since the distance from any point on the cylinder's surface to the $z$-axis equals $3,$ we must have $r=3$ for every point on the surface.

* On the other hand, $\theta $ can vary arbitrarily in its domain, and $z$ varies arbitrarily in the domain $z\in [0,3].$

Therefore, the equation of the surface in cylindrical polar coordinates is $r=3,$ where $(\theta ,z)\in [0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

decision.explanation: On C, r=3 and dA=dθ dz. The cost is (1/(2π))∫₀³∫₀²π(1+θ/π+2z) dθ dz = ∫₀³(2+2z) dz = 15 dollars.

after.worked_solution:
We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $$15.$

We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $$15.$

content.worked_solution:
We found that the surface of the heater can be described in cylindrical polar coordinates as

$$
r=3,\,(\theta ,z)\in C,
$$

where
$C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Hence, the cost to manufacture its mesh is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A
$$

Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{C}\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A.
$$

The function under the first integral is constant, so we have

$$
{∬}_{C}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(C)=2\pi \cdot 3=6\pi .
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $z.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}\frac{\theta }{\pi }\,\text{d}A & =\frac{(3-0)}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }\cdot {[{\theta }^{2}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{2\pi }((2\pi )^{2}-0) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $\theta .$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C}2z\,\text{d}A & =(2\pi -0){\int }_{0}^{3}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\pi ({3}^{2}-0) \\  & =18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi }{∬}_{C}(1+\frac{\theta }{\pi }+2z)\,\text{d}A=\frac{1}{2\pi }(6\pi +6\pi +18\pi )=15.
$$

Therefore, the cost to manufacture the mesh of the cylindrical heater is $$15.$

decision.explanation: Cylindrical coordinates give x=r cos(θ). Since r=3, the missing component is 3 cos(θ), which ensures x²+y²=9.

after.worked_solution:
Recall that the circle

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1
$$

in the $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9}+\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9} \\  & =\frac{9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{9}+\frac{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{9} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $(\theta ,z)\in C$ and $C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

Recall that the circle

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1
$$

in the $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9}+\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9} \\  & =\frac{9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{9}+\frac{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{9} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $(\theta ,z)\in C$ and $C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

content.worked_solution:
Recall that the circle

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1
$$

in the $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ),
$$

since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9}+\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}{9} \\  & =\frac{9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{9}+\frac{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{9} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $(\theta ,z)\in C$ and $C=[0,2\pi )\times [0,3].$

decision.explanation: The outward normal is radial: (x,y,0). On E, x²+y²=9, so its length is 3. Dividing by 3 gives the unit normal (x/3,y/3,0), which is perpendicular to the circle's tangent and lies within the plane z=2.

after.worked_solution:
We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
f(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z⟩\,(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $r(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
r(\theta )=f(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $r(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
r(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{r}^{′}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{′}(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{n}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{n}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{||\overset{~}{n}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
f(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z⟩\,(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $r(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
r(\theta )=f(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $r(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
r(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{r}^{′}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{′}(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{n}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{n}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{||\overset{~}{n}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We found that a parametrization of the cylinder is given by

$$
f(\theta ,z)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z⟩\,(\theta ,z)\in C.
$$

Restricting the parametrization of the cylinder to $z=2,$ we get a parametrization $r(\theta )$ for the heating element:

$$
r(\theta )=f(\theta ,2)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,2⟩
$$

For convenience, we express $r(\theta )$ in column vector column:

$$
r(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ z(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Notice that this curve is traversed *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

To calculate the outward-pointing unit normal vector to this curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1:** We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(\theta ).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(\theta ),$ we get

$$
{r}^{′}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {y}^{′}(\theta ) \\ {z}^{′}(\theta )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2:** Since $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $\frac{\pi }{2}$ radians clockwise $(ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2})$ to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

Using the hint, the rotation matrix corresponding to a $ϕ=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise rotation about the $z$-axis is

$$
{R}_{z}(\theta )=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(\theta )$ by $-\frac{\pi }{2}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
\overset{~}{n}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, we normalize the vector found in Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}||\overset{~}{n}|| & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{||\overset{~}{n}||} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}x(\theta ) \\ y(\theta ) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The flux integrand is F·n=(6y)(x/3)+x(y/3)=7xy/3. Thus the flux is ∮_E (7xy/3) ds.

after.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $E$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $E$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{E}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit vector to $E.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094056/assets/2cd5e4c7ab86cdb999e239e986713a51c07b8decb629b1ee4a656077590f04bb.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{E}(6y\,i+x\,j)\cdot (\frac{x}{3}\,i+\frac{y}{3}\,j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{E}2xy+\frac{1}{3}xy\,\text{d}s \\  & ={∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$
after.html:
If F is a vector field and E is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across E is given by ∮EF⋅nds, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit vector to E.
In our case, we have ∮EF⋅nds=∮E(6yi+xj)⋅(x3i+y3j)ds=∮E2xy+13xyds=∮E73xyds.

after.worked_solution:
We will evaluate the integral

$$
{∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s
$$

found in step 6 using the formula

$$
{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

with the parametrization of the curve $E$ given by

$$
r(\theta )=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi .
$$

As we found previously, ${r}^{′}(\theta )=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}^{′}(\theta )|| & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)=\frac{7}{3}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(\theta )) & =\frac{7}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =63{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta . \\  & =\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{63}{2}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We will evaluate the integral

$$
{∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s
$$

found in step 6 using the formula

$$
{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

with the parametrization of the curve $E$ given by

$$
r(\theta )=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi .
$$

As we found previously, ${r}^{′}(\theta )=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}^{′}(\theta )|| & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)=\frac{7}{3}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(\theta )) & =\frac{7}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =63{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta . \\  & =\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{63}{2}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We will evaluate the integral

$$
{∮}_{E}\frac{7}{3}xy\,\text{d}s
$$

found in step 6 using the formula

$$
{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

with the parametrization of the curve $E$ given by

$$
r(\theta )=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi .
$$

As we found previously, ${r}^{′}(\theta )=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}^{′}(\theta )|| & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x,y)=\frac{7}{3}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(\theta )) & =\frac{7}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{E}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(\theta ))\,‖{r}^{′}(\theta )‖\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =63{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta . \\  & =\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{63}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{63}{2}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{63}{4}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
